messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] potential problem with type = 3
messages.body_plain:
Hi Henrick,

Apologies for the delayed reply; you happened to post your email to
the list on the day my first child was born, so my availability has
been rather limited of late!

You've stumbled on a bug that is rather embarrassing for me: one of
the big features introduced in ez3.0 was the ability to specify type=3
in the call to ezANOVA, and yet I appear to have hard-coded all
subsequent calls to car::Anova() with type=2!

Until the next release of ez, you can fix this by grabbing the latest
versions of ezANOVA.R
(https://github.com/mike-lawrence/ez/blob/master/R/ezANOVA.R) and
ez-internal.R (https://github.com/mike-lawrence/ez/blob/master/R/ez-internal.R)
from github then source them after loading up ez the regular way:

library(ez)
source('ezANOVA.R')
source('ez-internal.R')

Cheers,

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology
Dalhousie University

Looking to arrange a meeting? Check my public calendar:
http://tr.im/mikes_public_calendar

~ Certainty is folly... I think. ~

messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] Help interpreting ezANOVA results for mixed designs
messages.subject_clean: [ez4r] Help interpreting ezANOVA results for mixed designs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

When one runs an ANOVA with multiple variables, regardless of whether
they're within or between, most software will produce multiple rows of
output corresponding to the tests of the main effects of each variable
as well as the interactions between the variables (2-way interactions,
3-way interactions, etc). In your case, I presume that you're looking
at the top-most rows of the anova output where the tests of the main
effects is printed. If, as you suggest, one row shows a "significant"
effect and the other row doesn't, this means that the former variable
has a "significant" main effect while the latter variable does not. It
is important to look further down the rows however, as these main
effects may be qualified by higher-order interactions between the
variables.

Mike

On Wed, Apr 20, 2011 at 3:39 PM, Ben Watson <wat...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I see that in a mixed design with both within and between variables,
> the effects involving the between variables are shown on two lines.
> These two lines are not the same, that is they will have different DF,
> F, p, etc.
>
> What is the difference between these two lines, and what do the
> differences between them mean? E.g., if the effect is significant in
> one case and not in the other, what is the applied meaning?
>
> Thanks,
>
> Ben.

messages.subject: Which analysis should I use?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

First of all, thanks for providing ezpackage, this is really great!
However, as ezpackage is giving me so many options, I'm wondering now,
which implementation is right for my setting:

I have 4 different groups (treatments) with 50 participants each. Each
participant's action is observed 5 times under the same condition. I
get the 5 values within one "round", where each participant has to
click 5 times at arbitrary moments.
I know that the different values for each participant are not
independent of each other. However, time effects are not of interest
for me and I don't assume that learning effects are apparent. I just
monitor 5 values for each participant in order to get more data. All
the data within one group (for all users) is then taken together and
an aggregated measure is calculated. Now the question is, whether
there are significant differences for this measure between the groups.
As there is no unbiased estimator for the measure and as my data is
not normal, I know that I need some form of sampling.

I've got two main questions:
First, I'm not sure whether bootstrapping or permutation tests seem to
be more appropriate.
Second, could I "ignore" the repeated measures and permute all values
together without regard to the participants who provided it? If not,
could I take vectors for each participant or user vector norms
instead?

What happens if I have an unbalanced design (when some answers are
missing)?

Thank you so much for your help!
Patricia

messages.subject: Re: Which analysis should I use?
messages.body_plain:
ANOVA don't require the data to be normal - just the residuals of the
model. It can be problematic to ignore the repeated measures - not
least because you would lose information and statistical power. It can
also introduce biases in some cases.

I'd start with RM ANOVA and look at residual plots ... and maybe
consider a transformation. Not familiar with the permutation options
yet ... these are tricky for repeated measures and I'm not sure how ez
does it.

Thom

messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] potential problem with type = 3
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

thanks for getting back to this issue and providing a fix. With this fix now ez computes type 3 sums. However, there is still an issue that I think is debatable. It relates to the way that ez computes the type 3 SSs in comparison to how SPSS (and probably SAS) do it.

At first, I think it would be great if one could get the same results in R as in SPSS, as SPSS is the de facto standard in our field (i.e., psychology).

What ez now returns as type 3 sum of squares is only identical to the SPSS results for within subjects effects for the highest order interaction, for the lower ones it diverges (sometimes massively).

Takethe example I already presented in my previous mail. There are 2 within subject factors: type with 3 levels and problem (=prob) with 2 levels. Furthermore one between subjects factor (instr) with 2 levels resulting in a: 2 (between) x 3 (within) x 2 (within) so called split-plot ANOVA. The following table (hopefully readable) compares the F-values from both programs. Furthermore, the last column gives the F-values of type 2 SS (they are identical in ez and SPSS):

| Effect          |   F-ez | F-SPSS | same? | Type II |
|-----------------+--------+--------+-------+---------|
| instr           |  0.005 |  0.005 | yes   |   0.005 |
| prob            | 50.871 | 87.128 | no    |  85.653 |
| instr:prob      | 19.782 | 19.782 | yes   |  19.782 |
| type            |  4.624 | 29.319 | no    |  29.433 |
| instr:type      |  3.831 |  3.831 | yes   |   3.831 |
| prob:type       |  1.059 | 63.933 | no    |  64.542 |
| instr:prob:type |  4.845 |  4.845 | yes   |   4.845 |
|-----------------+--------+--------+-------+---------|
(instr = between 2 levels; prob = within 2 levels; type = within 3 levels)

Here one can easily see the differences for lower level interactions and main effects for the type 3 SS. They are huge. Furthermore, the SPSS results for type 2 and type 3 sums are pretty much comparable overall. They differ only slightly. When one looks at this, the type 3 SS don't seem to be so unreasonable at all. (interestingly the results that match between ez and spps are also identical to the type 2 results..)

The differences are probably related to the way which terms are included in computing the type 3 sums. SPSS help says:
"The Type III sum of squares for an effect F can best be described as the sum of squares for F adjusted for effects that do not contain it, and orthogonal to effects (if any) that contain it."

To further nail this down, I tried to get the same results from SPSS that ez returns for the lower terms, but failed to obtain them.

My idea would be, that if one asks for type 3 sums in ez one (at least me) would expect to obtain the results that spss would give for this case. As this is what most people report in their papers if they talk about ANOVAs.

What do you respectively other list members think about that?

Let me finally add two things:

1. All the best to you and your family. It is great to hear that young scientists find the time to start a family.

2. ez is really great. Before knowing and regularly using ez, I always switched back to SPSS just for calculating ANOVAs. Your package made this step obsolete. ez is one of the few packages I use in almost all projects. Thank you for taking your time and producing this for the community.

Best,

Henrik

messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] potential problem with type = 3
messages.body_plain:
I tracked down the difference to 2 sources:

1) ez treats numeric between variables as numeric (thus fitting linear
effects when that variable is involved in an effect) whereas you
probably have told SPSS to treat your numeric variable "instruction"
as categorical. To make R treat "instruction" as categorical, convert
it to a factor.

2) SPSS seems to be set up with sum contrasts by default, whereas R
uses treatment contrasts by default. To make R use sum contrasts by
default, run: options(contrasts=c('contr.sum','contr.poly'))

In future versions of ez I'll provide an easier way to ask for
different contrasts and put some description of SPSS's default
behaviour.

> > | instr:prob:type |  4.845 |  4.845 | yes   |   4.845 |
> > |-----------------+--------+--------+-------+---------|
> > (instr = between 2 levels; prob = within 2 levels; type = within 3 levels)
> >
> > Here one can easily see the differences for lower level interactions and
> > main effects for the type 3 SS. They are huge. Furthermore, the SPSS results
> > for type 2 and type 3 sums are pretty much comparable overall. They differ
> > only slightly. When one looks at this, the type 3 SS don't seem to be so
> > unreasonable at all. (interestingly the results that match between ez and
> > spps are also identical to the type 2 results..)
> >
> > The differences are probably related to the way which terms are included in
> > computing the type 3 sums. SPSS help says:
> > "The Type III sum of squares for an effect F can best be described as the
> > sum of squares for F adjusted for effects that do not contain it, and
> > orthogonal to effects (if any) that contain it."
> >
> > To further nail this down, I tried to get the same results from SPSS that ez
> > returns for the lower terms, but failed to obtain them.
> >
> > My idea would be, that if one asks for type 3 sums in ez one (at least me)
> > would expect to obtain the results that spss would give for this case. As
> > this is what most people report in their papers if they talk about ANOVAs.
> >
> > What do you respectively other list members think about that?
> >
> > Let me finally add two things:
> >
> > 1. All the best to you and your family. It is great to hear that young

> >

messages.subject: How is ges determined?
messages.body_plain:
I'm tidying up the (final, I hope) draft of my book. As it happens the
earlier draft included a section on ges and also used ez to illustrate
some analyses. Having finally managed to upgrade to ez 3.0 on my mac I
now realize that you included ges.

For one-way designs you treat the subjects factor as a measured
factor. In this case both ges and and ez settle on the eta-squared
statistic (not partial eta-squared) as they should. I presume that you
have therefore treated all subjects and by-subjects effects as
measured. How do you deal with factors and covariates in more complex
designs? ez can not code the manipulated vs. measured factor
distinction.

I presume that it defaults to treating them as manipulated - or
perhaps manipulated for within and measured for between? What about
covariates (presumably mreasured)? Ideally there should be an option
to specify each factor individually ... an automatic solution will
always cause problems.

Thom

messages.body_plain:
ezANOVA has an argument called "observed" that lets you tell it which
of the arguments specified amongst "within" and "between" are observed
variables. Otherwise all variables are considered manipulated.

experiments. R package version 3.0-0.

@Manual{rJava,
